Write a note to a friend about a book you have been reading. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Dear Margaret,

You asked me last week what I had been reading, and I put you off with some vague answer, so here is the proper one. I have been working through an old memoir of a woman who kept house on the edge of a lumber camp in the 1890s. I found it in a box at the church sale for a quarter, and I believe it was the best quarter I ever spent.

She is not a grand writer, and I think that is why I like her. She tells things just as they happened and doesn't dress them up. There is a chapter about a peddler who came through in the dead of winter with a cart full of tin pans and a cough that she didn't like the sound of. Her husband wanted to send him on his way, but she gave him a bed by the stove and a bowl of soup, and he stayed eleven days. By the end of it he had mended every pot in the house, taught her boys a card game she disapproved of, and left behind a bundle of ribbon "for the trouble." She doesn't say what she thought of him. She only says that the pans lasted twenty years.

Then there is the cow. You would laugh at the cow. Her name was Duchess, and she was the most ill-tempered creature that ever walked on four legs. She would give milk only when it suited her, and she once followed the preacher halfway to town because she disliked his hat. The author treats her with such grave respect that I found myself taking Duchess's side in every argument.

What struck me most is how much hardship she passes over in a single sentence. A child sick with fever, a barn lost to fire, a whole season of poor crops, and then she goes straight on to something about the neighbor's goat. I don't think she was cold. I think she simply had no time to sit and mourn, and so she wrote it down the way she lived it, one thing after another.

I am about two-thirds through and rather dreading the end. If you would like it, I will mail it to you when I am done. The binding is loose and a few pages have a coffee ring, but I believe you would enjoy it as I have.

Do write and tell me what you have been reading. And come for tea when the weather turns, if the roads allow.

Affectionately yours,
Ellen
